parallel.requirements: Recognized the flat dataset, root /output/test15.rs, Cargo project, std-only requirement, exact stdout matching, path normalization, scheme lowercasing, port normalization, and validity behavior from black-box probes.
parallel.plan_and_ownership: Parent spawned one probe_binary child but continued owning probing, implementation, build, and verification itself; the child independently pursued the same implementation in the same /output workspace.
parallel.implementation: Parent implemented modules normalize/render/url and a root test15.rs using simple Rust parsing with args[3].parse().unwrap(); child later implemented a different module set with parse.rs and stoi-style parsing.
parallel.integration_and_delivery: Both parent and child wrote the same required Cargo.toml, src/lib.rs, url_parser module files, and root test15.rs. The parent did not merge a returned child result; the shared output tree ended with overlapping provenance.
parallel.verification: Parent built with Cargo, fixed a direct rustc re-export error, rebuilt, compared documented and edge cases, checked no-argument exit behavior, and listed binaries after interrupting the child.
parallel.unfinished_or_incorrect: Official evaluation still failed 1 of 40. The parent also closed after child overwrites without rerunning the same behavioral comparisons on the child-modified final tree.

serial.requirements: Recognized the flat dataset, root /output/test15.rs, Cargo project, std-only requirement, exact stdout matching, path normalization, scheme-empty rendering, host-or-path validity, and std::stoi-style port parsing.
serial.plan_and_ownership: One serial actor owned the entire path from dataset inspection through probing, implementation, compilation, verification, and final report with no delegation or subagent activity.
serial.implementation: Implemented a std-only Cargo package named test15_migration with cli parsing, url_parser path and url modules, a root test15.rs entrypoint, and explicit parse_port_argument logic approximating std::stoi.
serial.integration_and_delivery: Created the final project once in /output and built both /output/test15 and target/release/test15 without concurrent writers or handoff integration.
serial.verification: Compiled both standalone and Cargo binaries, then compared outputs with process substitution on documented examples, empty scheme/host cases, negative ports, query-only/fragment-only invalid cases, and stoi plus/trailing/space cases.
serial.unfinished_or_incorrect: Official evaluation still failed 1 of 40 despite the broader stoi-targeted verification, so an ordinary hidden semantic gap remained.

comparison_dimensions.parallel_summary: Parallel recognized the required CLI and output fields and inferred many formatting rules from the reference executable.
comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: Serial recognized the same prompt requirements and explicitly identified std::stoi-style parsing as part of matching the C++ harness.
comparison_dimensions.difference: Both covered the same task surface, but serial captured stoi parsing more explicitly while parallel's parent implementation used plain Rust parse before the child wrote a different parser.

comparison_dimensions.parallel_summary: Parent spawned /root/probe_binary but also performed the main probing, implementation, build, and verification itself.
comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: Serial kept one owner for probing, implementing, compiling, verifying, and reporting.
comparison_dimensions.difference: Parallel duplicated implementation ownership across parent and child, while serial had no cross-agent ownership split.

comparison_dimensions.parallel_summary: The child received a delegated probing task but operated in the same output workspace and produced an implementation without a visible ownership boundary for the deliverable files.
comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: Serial had no inter-agent brief or handoff; all discoveries stayed in one actor's context through implementation and verification.
comparison_dimensions.difference: The parallel run had a weak shared-output boundary, but there is not enough evidence that a missing requirement in the child brief, rather than overlapping live writes, was the primary defect.

comparison_dimensions.parallel_summary: Parent implemented normalize/render/url modules and a root entrypoint; child implemented parse/url modules with tests and stoi-style parsing.
comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: Serial implemented cli.rs, path.rs, url.rs, and root test15.rs in one pass with explicit stoi-style parsing.
comparison_dimensions.difference: Parallel had two implementation variants in the same output tree, while serial had one internally consistent variant.

comparison_dimensions.parallel_summary: Parent waited for the child twice, listed it as still running, then interrupted it before any normal child handoff.
comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: Serial had no child result lifecycle; the single actor completed its own tests and final answer.
comparison_dimensions.difference: Parallel had an interrupted child lifecycle after the child had already modified /output, while serial had no result retrieval or interruption issue.

comparison_dimensions.parallel_summary: Parent and child both wrote the required /output Cargo project and root entrypoint, and the child compiled after its overlapping writes.
comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: Serial wrote the output project once and did not share implementation files with a live child.
comparison_dimensions.difference: This is the material coordination difference: parallel created an uninspected mixed-provenance deliverable; serial avoided shared-state collision.

comparison_dimensions.parallel_summary: Parent verified its own candidate on documented and probed cases before the child wrote and compiled a different overlapping candidate.
comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: Serial verified the same final project it had just built, including extra stoi-style cases and query-only/fragment-only invalid cases.
comparison_dimensions.difference: Parallel's verification no longer cleanly established the provenance of the final shared output after the child write; serial's checks applied to its single final tree.

comparison_dimensions.parallel_summary: Parallel spent extra time and tokens on overlapping parent and child work, waited twice, interrupted the child, then closed with the parent final answer.
comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: Serial spent a comparable wall-clock budget but no subagent budget, finished after verification, and had a lower token footprint.
comparison_dimensions.difference: Parallel coordination increased duplicate work and closure complexity without improving the official outcome; both remained 39/40 failures.

outcome_analysis.explanation: The current completed official evaluations show no discordant outcome: parallel and serial both failed with 39/40 tests passed. The concrete task-solving difference is process-level, not score-level: parallel had overlapping live writers to the required deliverable, while serial had one coherent owner. Both implementations still missed one hidden evaluator case.
parallel_contributors: Overlapping parent and child implementation writes created an uninspected final-output provenance problem.
serial_contributors: Serial avoided coordination conflicts by keeping probing, implementation, build, and verification in one actor.
ordinary_implementation_differences: Parallel parent used plain Rust integer parsing in the implementation it verified; the child and serial implementations included a stoi-style parser, but both official outcomes were still 39/40.
outcome_analysis.causal_scope: No outcome difference; retained pattern is a realized parallel-side adverse process effect, not an explanation for a discordant score.

candidates.reason: Implementation owner was not missing: both parent and child actively implemented, and the defect was overlapping ownership rather than absence of an implementer.
The run did not divide separate compatible components needing an integration owner; the observed issue was same deliverable writes in /output.
The parent assembled and built a deliverable, and the child also assembled one; assembly was duplicated rather than unowned.
The parent executed the end-to-end path from probing to build and tests; the failure is not lack of pipeline ownership.
Implementation was not blocked behind a mandatory serial preflight; parent and child both probed and implemented while the other was active.
The parent did not defer all productive work until a completed investigation phase; it implemented while the child was still running.
The critical implementation path was not starved; parent and child both spent capacity on implementation and verification.
There was only one child and no collective fan-out or retry breadth exhausting the run budget before closure.

Although the child did substantial work and was interrupted, the directly evidenced adverse event was overlapping deliverable writes, not an overbroad child assignment leaving indispensable work undone.
The child understood the migration, probed the binary, wrote a Cargo project, and built it; no already-known requirement omission is proven as the cause of unusable work.
The child and parent were not producing separate components with an interface mismatch; they wrote the same required project files, so the write label is more specific.
No transferred finding is shown to disappear through summary or compaction before a receiver repeats or misuses the work.
There was no large returned handoff that the parent failed to reduce; the child was interrupted before a normal result handoff.
The parent did not consume a child handoff describing superseded state; the child wrote directly to /output and was interrupted.
No incompatible reports reached the parent and remained unadjudicated; the conflict is concrete same deliverable writes, handled under Concurrent Writes.

The parent did make a final completion claim after local checks, but the directly evidenced boundary was a child deliverable overwrite; there is no separate parent-visible integrated mismatch to label independently.
There was no replacement or retry agent repeating prior work without inherited checkpoints; only the original parent and one child were active.

A child implementation write occurred after parent verification, but that is the consequence of the same deliverable overwrite episode, not a separate retained timing pattern.
The child did not return a completed retrievable implementation for the parent to join; it wrote directly into /output and was interrupted.
The delegated child was not a verifier producing a trapped finding; it implemented and built overlapping files.
The child was interrupted, but the parent had already taken over implementation and verification; any missing child recovery is downstream of the write/provenance collision.
No concrete completed child result was returned and visible for the parent to inspect or ignore; the child was interrupted.
The parent waited twice and checked agent status, but the adverse event was the child write to the deliverable, not a distinct wait episode with separate consequence.
The agents did not merely write different files claiming overlapping behavior; the child wrote the same required entrypoint/project deliverable, so Deliverable Overwrite is more specific.

The serial run had one writer for the final deliverable.
